name: Drafting Statements and Disclosures
title: Drafting Statements and Disclosures
answer: Drafting statements and disclosures covers the preparation of financial statements, management discussion and analysis, risk factors, notes to accounts, and regulatory filings such as annual reports and prospectuses. It also includes routine disclosures like earnings releases, ESG metrics, and compliance updates. The work sits between accounting, legal, and investor relations, where language must be precise and consistent with the underlying numbers. AI assistance here focuses on generating first drafts, summarizing source material, and checking that figures and wording match across documents.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting statements and disclosures covers the preparation of financial statements, management discussion and analysis, risk factors, notes to accounts, and regulatory filings such as annual reports and prospectuses. It also includes routine disclosures like earnings releases, ESG metrics, and compliance updates. The work sits between accounting, legal, and investor relations, where language must be precise and consistent with the underlying numbers. AI assistance here focuses on generating first drafts, summarizing source material, and checking that figures and wording match across documents.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work typically runs on secure document platforms connected to a company's general ledger, prior filings, and internal policy libraries. Large language models are used with retrieval over approved source documents so that drafts reflect the company's own accounting policies and historical language. Because financial data is sensitive, deployments are usually private cloud or on-premises, with access controls and audit logging. No external model should see unpublished figures without explicit controls.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common workflow starts by pulling structured data from the ledger and unstructured text from prior disclosures, then using a model to draft sections against a template. The system cross-checks totals, dates, and defined terms between the draft and source tables, flagging mismatches for review. Human accountants and lawyers then edit the draft, with the model suggesting alternative wording or identifying missing disclosure items. The final version is version-controlled so every change can be traced.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Accuracy and confidentiality are the main risks, since a wrong figure or leaked draft can have regulatory and market consequences. Organizations need clear rules on who can approve AI-drafted text, what data may be used for training or retrieval, and how provenance is recorded for each sentence. Disclosure controls should require human sign-off before any filing leaves the company, and audit trails should show which model version and source documents were used. This is a matter of internal policy and professional standards rather than legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous drafting that updates disclosures as soon as new ledger data or regulatory changes arrive, rather than waiting for quarter-end. Agentic systems may eventually assemble entire draft filings from approved components and then run a checklist of disclosure requirements. XBRL tagging and machine-readable statements will likely become more automated, with drafts generated already tagged for regulators. Human review will remain the final control, but the reviewer's job will shift from writing to verifying and approving.
